extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students in real analysis / Fourier analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and convergence criteria for the Weierstrass approximation theorem and for Fourier series (definitions, kernels, convergence tests, inequalities, uniqueness and Parseval). Includes construction via approximate identities and analysis of Dirichlet/Fejér kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate identity (definition / required properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of functions {ϕ_n} on an interval (e.g. [−R,R] or [−1,1]) is an approximate identity if it satisfies: (i) ϕ_n(x) ≥ 0 for all x; (ii) ∫ ϕ_n(x) dx = 1 for each n (total mass 1); (iii) for every δ>0, sup_{|x|≥δ} ϕ_n(x) → 0 as n → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret ϕ as a localized mass distribution: if most mass concentrates near 0 and total mass is 1 then convolutions f * ϕ_n produce averages of nearby translates of f and can approximate f. Property (iii) is used to control the contribution from far-away translates. The text constructs polynomial ϕ_n with these properties to make convolution produce polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weierstrass Approximation Theorem (statement and method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any complex-valued continuous function on a bounded interval [a,b] is the uniform limit of a sequence of polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: reduce to [0,1] via affine changes, extend f to be zero outside [0,1], then convolve f with a polynomial approximate identity ϕ_n to obtain P_n(x)=∫ f(x−t)ϕ_n(t) dt. Show each P_n is a polynomial (because ϕ_n is a polynomial and integrals of monomials yield polynomials) and P_n → f uniformly using uniform continuity of f and properties (i)-(iii) of ϕ_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and properties of the specific polynomial approximate identity ϕ_n (Lemma 1.51 and following)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose ϕ_n(x) = c_n (1 − (x/R)^2)^n supported on [−R,R] with c_n chosen so total integral equals 1. Lemma asserts existence and growth bounds on c_n (used to verify properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show c_n is finite and estimate it (the lemma provides an upper bound for c_n for large n). Use these estimates to verify (i) nonnegativity, (ii) total integral 1, and (iii) concentration of mass near 0: for any δ>0, sup_{|x|≥δ} ϕ_n(x) → 0 as n→∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Fourier series and Fourier coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For a 2π-periodic, Riemann-integrable function f on [−π,π], the Fourier series is ∑_{n=−∞}^∞ c_n e^{inx} with Fourier coefficients c_n = (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} f(x) e^{−inx} dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the trigonometric series converges uniformly to f, the coefficients must equal these integrals. The real-form coefficients (a_n,b_n) are given by the usual cosine/sine integrals. For different periods replace 2π by 2ℓ suitably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial sums expressed as convolution with Dirichlet kernel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Nth partial sum s_N(f,x) = ∑_{n=−N}^N c_n e^{inx} equals (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} f(x−t) D_N(t) dt, where D_N is the Dirichlet kernel D_N(t)=∑_{n=−N}^N e^{int}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convolution identity is used to analyze convergence behavior. It follows from termwise integration and periodicity. Because D_N is not an approximate identity, this representation explains subtle convergence issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirichlet kernel explicit formula and its failure as approximate identity
rubrics_metrics.description: D_N(x) = sin((N + 1/2)x)/sin(x/2) (equivalently the geometric-sum expression); and ∫_{−π}^{π} (1/2π) D_N(x) dx = 1 but D_N(x) does not tend to 0 for fixed x≠0 as N→∞, so D_N is not an approximate identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because D_N has large oscillations and does not vanish off 0, convolution with D_N (i.e., partial sums) need not converge pointwise or uniformly, which is the source of subtleties in Fourier convergence theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 1.53 (L2 best approximation / coefficients minimize L^2 error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among all trigonometric polynomials ∑_{n=−N}^N d_n e^{inx}, the L^2([−π,π]) distance ∫ |f(x) − ∑ d_n e^{inx}|^2 dx is uniquely minimized by choosing d_n = c_n (the Fourier coefficients). The minimal value equals ∫ |f|^2 dx − ∑_{n=−N}^N |c_n|^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This characterizes Fourier coefficients as orthogonal projections in L^2; the theorem underpins Bessel/Parseval and shows partial sums are best L^2 approximants for that truncation level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bessel's inequality (Corollary 1.54)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ L^2([−π,π]) has Fourier coefficients c_n, then ∑_{n=−∞}^∞ |c_n|^2 ≤ (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} |f(x)|^2 dx; in particular the coefficient sequence is square-summable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from Theorem 1.53 by letting N→∞ and observing nonnegativity of the L^2 error. Use in deriving Riemann–Lebesgue and other results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riemann–Lebesgue Lemma (Corollary 1.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ L^1([−π,π]) (or Riemann integrable on [−π,π]) then its Fourier coefficients c_n → 0 as |n|→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from Bessel's inequality (square-summability implies coefficients tend to 0). Provides necessary decay but not rate; stronger regularity gives quantitative decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smoothness implies coefficient decay and uniform convergence (two derivatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is 2π-periodic and has two continuous derivatives, then |c_n| ≤ C / n^2 and the Fourier series converges uniformly (Weierstrass M-test using the n^{-2} bound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain by integrating by parts twice: c_n = (1/(in)^2)(1/2π) ∫ f''(x) e^{−inx} dx. The result shows higher smoothness yields faster coefficient decay and better convergence properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1.56 (one derivative suffices for uniform convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a 2π-periodic function f has one continuous derivative, then its Fourier series converges uniformly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses c_n = (1/in) d_n where d_n are Fourier coefficients of f', then Schwarz and Bessel inequalities yield ∑ |c_n| uniformly summable; apply Weierstrass M-test. Dini's test is later used to show convergence is to f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dini's test for pointwise convergence (Theorem 1.57)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f be 2π-periodic and Riemann integrable. Fix x. If there exist constants δ>0 and M<∞ such that a local regularity condition (given in the text) holds near x (the condition is satisfied in particular if f is differentiable at x), then s_N(f,x) → f(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Dini condition is a local integrability/regularity condition on the symmetric difference of f about x; differentiability at x suffices. Proof reduces to showing convolution with Dirichlet kernel tends to f using Riemann–Lebesgue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fejér kernel (definition, formula) and its approximate-identity properties (Lemma 1.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fejér kernel K_N is the Cesàro (arithmetic) mean of Dirichlet kernels: K_N = (1/(N+1)) ∑_{n=0}^N D_n. Lemma gives an explicit closed form for K_N and shows K_N ≥ 0, (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} K_N(x) dx = 1, and for any δ>0, sup_{|x|≥δ} K_N(x) → 0 (i.e., K_N is an approximate identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because K_N is nonnegative and concentrates mass near 0, convolution with K_N (Cesàro sums) yields good approximation properties even when Dirichlet convolution fails. The lemma's explicit formula is used to verify the three approximate-identity properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fejér's Theorem (Theorem 1.59) — Cesàro convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is 2π-periodic and Riemann integrable and is continuous at x_0, then the Cesàro (Fejér) means (the arithmetic means of partial sums) converge to f(x_0): lim_{N→∞} (1/(N+1)) ∑_{n=0}^N s_n(f,x_0) = f(x_0). If f is uniformly continuous on a set E, convergence is uniform for x_0 in E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses K_N as an approximate identity and the three properties from Lemma 1.58. Fejér's theorem shows Cesàro summation regularizes Fourier series and provides the best general convergence result for arbitrary continuous f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness theorems for Fourier series (Corollary 1.60 and Corollary 1.66)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two Riemann-integrable 2π-periodic functions f and g have the same Fourier coefficients, then f(x)=g(x) at every point of continuity of both. Moreover, if f has all Fourier coefficients 0, then (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} f(x) g(x) dx = 0 for every Riemann-integrable g; in particular (via density/approximation) f is zero in the L^2/inner-product sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Fejér's theorem to the difference f−g (or to f itself) and use approximation arguments (approximate identities) and Parseval to upgrade to integral/orthogonality conclusions. These results show Fourier coefficients determine the function up to issues on sets of discontinuity (pointwise) and in L^2 sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parseval's Theorem (Theorem 1.61)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is 2π-periodic and Riemann integrable with Fourier series ∑ c_n e^{inx} (in L^2 sense), then (1/2π) ∫_{−π}^{π} |f(x)|^2 dx = ∑_{n=−∞}^∞ |c_n|^2 (equality in Bessel's inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parseval is proved by approximating f in L^2 by continuous functions, applying the Fejér means, and passing to the limit. In the real-coefficient form, (1/2π) ∫ |f|^2 = (a_0^2)/2 + ∑ (a_n^2 + b_n^2). Parseval yields orthogonality and energy-equality interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristics / examples (sawtooth function) illustrating discontinuity effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The sawtooth function f(x) = (1/2)(π − x) on (0,2π) has Fourier series ∑ (sin nx)/n. Although the Fourier series converges pointwise to f, it does not converge uniformly due to the jump; coefficient decay is only order 1/n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This example shows (i) discontinuities permit pointwise convergence but preclude uniform convergence and fast coefficient decay; (ii) harmonic coefficients ~1/n is typical for functions with jump discontinuities; (iii) motivates importance of smoothness hypotheses for uniform convergence and decay rates.
